A. INTRODUCTION
1. THE AMERICAN PUBLIC LAW REMEDIAL SYSTEM
In this chapter and the chapter that follows, we focus on the structure 
of the pubhc law remedial system. There are several types of remfidifts 
available for allegedly unlawful behavior by government officials. The 
conventional remedies in contemporary federal public law are injunctions, 
often accompanied by a formal declaration of legal rights and obligations. A 
prominent report—tissued five years before the passage of the APA by 
Attorney General Robert Jackson’s CommitteA on Administrative 
Procedure—described the injunction as “the common remedy” and “the 
remedy normally used” in administrative actions. COKIM. ON Ad min . Pr o c .,

Judicial review in this injunctive mode is, in the usual case, expressly 
authorized by a statutory provision that establishes judicial jurisdiction, 
specifies the form and timing of review proceedings, indicates who can seek 
review, and empowers the reviewing court to affirm, reverse, or rAmand 
particular agency decisions. Sometimes an agency-specific statute authorizes 
review. Sometimes the challenge proceeds under the APA which is the most 
important statute for our purposes. In other cases, plaintifis proceed under 
more general grants of federal jurisdiction, such as 28 U.S.C. § 1331. The APA 
is not itself a grant of federal court jurisdiction. Rather, it is a statute that 
authorizes judicial review of agency action when jurisdiction otherwise exists 
under a different statute. It identifies who has the right to challenge agency 
action (section 702), the form and venue of proceeding with an a d ministra five 
challenge (section 703), the actions that can be reviewed (section 704) and the 
scope of review that a reviewing court is to apply (section 706). This chapter 
focuses on this last category—the scope of judicial review.
The social function of “judicial review” as we conceptualize it here is 
the maintenance of the rule of law, given the constraints on judicial 
authority inherent in a system committed also to a separation of 
governmental powers. Estabhshing the appropriate role of the reviewing 
court—its scope of review concerning the challenged administrative
